docs.title: CS371 Cloud Infrastructure — Docker Swarm
docs.text: Project: Pace University CS371 Path: docs/cloud-infra.md Last updated: November 3, 2026

docs.title: 1. Purpose and architecture
docs.text: This document records the two-node Docker Swarm environment configured for the CS371 project. It covers the manager, worker, Nebula networking, Registry, Visualizer, firewall hooks, and a two-replica test application.

docs.title: Node inventory
docs.text:
Role Hostname Nebula IP LAN IP observed Manager (Ryzen 0) cs371-bc9b0c 10.80.0.10 192.168.4.30 Worker (Ryzen 1) cs371-bc9a92 10.80.0.11 192.168.1.174

Docker Engine 29.1.3 was reported on both nodes. The Linux account is milkalmond on Ryzen 0 and twix on Ryzen 1.

flowchart TB
  Mac[Developer MacBook]
  subgraph Nebula[Private Nebula network 10.80.0.0/24]
    M[Ryzen 0 - Manager<br/>10.80.0.10]
    W[Ryzen 1 - Worker<br/>10.80.0.11]
  end
  Mac --> M
  Mac --> W
  M <-->|Swarm control and overlay traffic| W
  M --> R[Registry :5000]
  M --> V[Visualizer :8000]
  M --> A1[whoami replica]
  W --> A2[whoami replica]

docs.title: Required network ports
docs.text:
Port Protocol Purpose 2377 TCP Swarm manager/control-plane communication 7946 TCP/UDP Swarm node discovery and gossip 4789 UDP Swarm overlay VXLAN data path 5000 TCP Private Docker Registry 8000 TCP Docker Swarm Visualizer 8081 TCP Test application, published through Swarm ingress

The Nebula identity bayron is used in host-specific access rules. Keep the Registry, Visualizer, and test application restricted to the intended private-network clients.

docs.title: 2. Verify Docker and Swarm readiness
docs.text:
Docker was already installed on both machines when this configuration work began. The exact package installation transcript was not retained, so this document does not assume which package source was used.

Run on each node:

docker --version
sudo systemctl status docker --no-pager
sudo docker info

On the manager, check the cluster summary:

docker info --format 'Swarm: {{.Swarm.LocalNodeState}} | Manager IP: {{.Swarm.NodeAddr}} | Managers: {{.Swarm.Managers}} | Nodes: {{.Swarm.Nodes}}'

Observed manager state:

Swarm: active | Manager IP: 10.80.0.10 | Managers: 1 | Nodes: 2

docs.title: 3. Initialize the manager and join the worker
docs.text:
Ryzen 0 (cs371-bc9b0c) is the manager and leader. Its advertised Nebula address is 10.80.0.10.

For a new cluster only, initialize the manager:

sudo docker swarm init --advertise-addr 10.80.0.10

Do not run swarm init again on a node already in a Swarm. Check first:

sudo docker info --format '{{.Swarm.LocalNodeState}}'
docker node ls

Generate a worker join command on the manager:

docker swarm join-token worker

Run the generated command on Ryzen 1. Its endpoint should be 10.80.0.10:2377:

sudo docker swarm join --token <WORKER_JOIN_TOKEN> 10.80.0.10:2377

Replace the placeholder with the token generated by the manager. Never commit a real join token, password, or private key to the repository.

Verify membership on the manager:

docker node ls

Observed cluster:

Hostname Status Availability Manager status cs371-bc9b0c Ready Active Leader cs371-bc9a92 Ready Active Worker

docs.title: 4. Label the nodes
docs.text:
The nodes were labeled to identify their roles. Run on the manager:

docker node update --label-add cs371role=manager cs371-bc9b0c
docker node update --label-add cs371role=worker cs371-bc9a92

Inspect labels:

docker node inspect cs371-bc9b0c --format '{{.Description.Hostname}} {{json .Spec.Labels}}'
docker node inspect cs371-bc9a92 --format '{{.Description.Hostname}} {{json .Spec.Labels}}'

The test stack uses a spread placement preference based on node.labels.cs371role. This is a preference, not a hard placement constraint. Verify actual placement with docker service ps.

docs.title: 5. Nebula networking
docs.text:
Nebula provides the private mesh network. The observed addresses are:

  • Ryzen 0: 10.80.0.10/24 on tun0
  • Ryzen 1: 10.80.0.11/24 on tun0

Check the interface and service:

ip -4 addr show tun0
sudo systemctl status nebula --no-pager
sudo systemctl is-active nebula

Validate a configuration before applying it:

sudo nebula -config /etc/nebula/config.yml -test

Important: nebula -test validates the file; it does not apply changes to the running service. After a validated change, restart Nebula on the affected node:

sudo systemctl restart nebula
sudo systemctl is-active nebula

Restart one node at a time. An SSH session over Nebula may briefly disconnect; reconnect after the service is active.

docs.title: Swarm rules in Nebula
docs.text:
The manager's inbound policy includes these rules for the servers group:

    - port: 7946
      proto: tcp
      group: servers
    - port: 7946
      proto: udp
      group: servers
    - port: 4789
      proto: udp
      group: servers
    - port: 2377
      proto: tcp
      group: servers

The manager also has host-specific TCP access for Nebula host bayron on ports 5000, 8000, and 8081.

The worker's observed inbound policy includes:

  inbound:
    - port: any
      proto: icmp
      host: any
    - port: 22
      proto: tcp
      group: laptops
    - port: any
      proto: any
      group: servers
    - port: 8081
      proto: tcp
      host: bayron

The worker's broad servers rule is existing configuration. Review it with the team before narrowing it, because it can affect peer communication.

docs.title: 6. Private Docker Registry
docs.text:
A Registry v2 instance was running on Ryzen 0 using image registry:2. The observed Swarm service was:

NAME       MODE         REPLICAS   IMAGE
registry   replicated   1/1        registry:2

The Registry API was verified from the MacBook over Nebula:

curl -i --max-time 10 http://10.80.0.10:5000/v2/

Expected successful response:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Docker-Distribution-Api-Version: registry/2.0

{}

The exact original Registry creation command or stack file was not captured. Do not recreate the Registry blindly on an existing host; inspect the service/container and its storage configuration first.

docs.title: 7. Docker Swarm Visualizer
docs.text:
The Visualizer was run as a container on Ryzen 0 and bound to its Nebula IP:

docker pull dockersamples/visualizer:stable

docker run -d \
  --name visualizer \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  -p 10.80.0.10:8000:8080 \
  -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
  dockersamples/visualizer:stable

Verify:

docker ps --filter name=visualizer
docker logs --tail 30 visualizer

Open from a Nebula-connected client:

http://10.80.0.10:8000

The Visualizer displayed both Swarm nodes and their manager/worker roles.

Security: Mounting /var/run/docker.sock gives the container access to the Docker daemon. Restrict the Visualizer to trusted users and the private Nebula network. Do not expose port 8000 publicly.

docs.title: 8. Docker firewall configuration
docs.text: The Docker DOCKER-USER chain filters traffic forwarded to containers. The manager and worker have different interface configurations, so their scripts are documented separately.

docs.title: Manager (Ryzen 0)
docs.text:
Persistent script:

/usr/local/sbin/registry-firewall.sh

Observed contents:

#!/bin/bash
set -e

# Allow established connections to return.
iptables -C DOCKER-USER -m conntrack --ctstate RELATED,ESTABLISHED -j ACCEPT 2>/dev/null ||
iptables -I DOCKER-USER 1 -m conntrack --ctstate RELATED,ESTABLISHED -j ACCEPT

# Block new Registry connections arriving outside Nebula.
iptables -C DOCKER-USER ! -i tun0 -p tcp -m conntrack --ctorigdstport 5000 -j DROP 2>/dev/null ||
iptables -A DOCKER-USER ! -i tun0 -p tcp -m conntrack --ctorigdstport 5000 -j DROP

# Block new Visualizer connections arriving outside Nebula.
iptables -C DOCKER-USER ! -i tun0 -p tcp -m conntrack --ctorigdstport 8000 -j DROP 2>/dev/null ||
iptables -A DOCKER-USER ! -i tun0 -p tcp -m conntrack --ctorigdstport 8000 -j DROP

# Block new test application connections arriving outside Nebula.
iptables -C DOCKER-USER ! -i tun0 -p tcp -m conntrack --ctorigdstport 8081 -j DROP 2>/dev/null ||
iptables -A DOCKER-USER ! -i tun0 -p tcp -m conntrack --ctorigdstport 8081 -j DROP

Docker's systemd drop-in is:

/etc/systemd/system/docker.service.d/registry-firewall.conf

with:

[Service]
ExecStartPost=/usr/local/sbin/registry-firewall.sh

Inspect active rules and the startup hook:

sudo iptables -S DOCKER-USER
sudo systemctl show docker.service -p ExecStartPost --no-pager

docs.title: Worker (Ryzen 1)
docs.text:
The worker's physical LAN interface observed during setup was enp1s0f0 (192.168.1.174).

Persistent script:

/usr/local/sbin/swarm-test-firewall.sh

Observed contents:

#!/bin/bash
set -e

# Allow established connections.
iptables -C DOCKER-USER -m conntrack --ctstate RELATED,ESTABLISHED -j ACCEPT 2>/dev/null ||
iptables -I DOCKER-USER 1 -m conntrack --ctstate RELATED,ESTABLISHED -j ACCEPT

# Block test application access from the physical LAN.
iptables -C DOCKER-USER -i enp1s0f0 -p tcp -m conntrack --ctorigdstport 8081 -j DROP 2>/dev/null ||
iptables -A DOCKER-USER -i enp1s0f0 -p tcp -m conntrack --ctorigdstport 8081 -j DROP

The script is executable. The Docker systemd drop-in is:

/etc/systemd/system/docker.service.d/swarm-test-firewall.conf

with:

[Service]
ExecStartPost=/usr/local/sbin/swarm-test-firewall.sh

After creating the drop-in, systemd was reloaded:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload

Verify on the worker:

sudo iptables -S DOCKER-USER
sudo systemctl show docker.service -p ExecStartPost --no-pager

Firewall difference: The manager blocks new connections to ports 5000, 8000, and 8081 on interfaces other than tun0. The worker's documented rule blocks port 8081 arriving on its physical LAN interface. These policies are not identical. Do not flush DOCKER-USER or replace either policy without reviewing and testing the impact on Swarm overlay traffic.

docs.title: 9. Multi-node test application
docs.text:
The test application uses traefik/whoami, which returns the hostname and network details of the container handling the request.

Repository file:

deploy/swarm-test/compose.yaml

Contents:

services:
  whoami:
    image: traefik/whoami
    ports:
      - target: 80
        published: 8081
        protocol: tcp
        mode: ingress
    deploy:
      replicas: 2
      placement:
        preferences:
          - spread: node.labels.cs371role
      restart_policy:
        condition: on-failure
    networks:
      - swarm-test

networks:
  swarm-test:
    driver: overlay

docs.title: Validate and copy the file
docs.text:
From the repository root on the MacBook:

docker compose -f deploy/swarm-test/compose.yaml config
scp deploy/swarm-test/compose.yaml milkalmond@10.80.0.10:~/swarm-test-compose.yaml

docs.title: Deploy on the manager
docs.text:
ssh milkalmond@10.80.0.10
docker stack deploy -c ~/swarm-test-compose.yaml swarm-test

docs.title: Verify the stack and task placement
docs.text:
docker stack services swarm-test
docker service ps swarm-test_whoami --no-trunc

Observed service status:

NAME                MODE         REPLICAS   IMAGE
swarm-test_whoami   replicated   2/2        traefik/whoami:latest

The two tasks were observed on different nodes:

  • cs371-bc9b0c — manager
  • cs371-bc9a92 — worker

docs.title: Test from the MacBook
docs.text:
With the MacBook connected to Nebula:

curl -i --max-time 10 http://10.80.0.10:8081
curl -i --max-time 10 http://10.80.0.11:8081

Both endpoints returned HTTP/1.1 200 OK on November 3, 2026. The responses showed different container hostnames, confirming that both replicas were running and reachable.

The Compose file uses mode: ingress. Swarm's routing mesh makes the published port available through each node and can route a request to an available task. A request to a node IP does not prove that the task handling the request is located on that same node; use docker service ps to verify task placement.

docs.title: Check cluster membership
docs.text:
docker node ls
docker service ls
docker info --format 'Swarm: {{.Swarm.LocalNodeState}} | Manager IP: {{.Swarm.NodeAddr}} | Managers: {{.Swarm.Managers}} | Nodes: {{.Swarm.Nodes}}'

docs.title: Check Nebula
docs.text:
ip -4 addr show tun0
sudo systemctl is-active nebula

From the MacBook:

ping -c 4 10.80.0.10
ping -c 4 10.80.0.11

docs.title: Check Registry and Visualizer
docs.text:
curl -i --max-time 10 http://10.80.0.10:5000/v2/
docker ps --filter name=visualizer
docker logs --tail 30 visualizer

Visualizer URL: http://10.80.0.10:8000.

docs.title: Check the application
docs.text:
docker stack services swarm-test
docker service ps swarm-test_whoami --no-trunc
docker service logs swarm-test_whoami --tail 30
curl -i --max-time 10 http://10.80.0.10:8081
curl -i --max-time 10 http://10.80.0.11:8081

If local application tests work but the MacBook cannot connect, inspect the Nebula inbound TCP 8081 rule and confirm the running Nebula service has been restarted after the configuration change. nebula -test alone does not apply the change.

Before restarting services or changing firewall rules, inspect:

sudo iptables -S DOCKER-USER
sudo systemctl is-active nebula
sudo systemctl show docker.service -p ExecStartPost --no-pager

Do not flush firewall rules as a troubleshooting shortcut.

docs.title: Remove only the test stack
docs.text:
If the team intentionally wants to remove the test application:

docker stack rm swarm-test

This removes the test stack, not the Registry or Visualizer.

docs.title: 11. Security and operational notes
docs.text:
• Keep the manager endpoint, Registry, Visualizer, and test application on the intended private Nebula network.
  • Never commit Nebula private keys, passwords, Swarm join tokens, or other secrets.
  • The Visualizer's Docker socket mount is privileged; restrict access to it.
  • Do not expose the Docker daemon API over an unauthenticated TCP port.
  • Preserve Swarm communication ports: TCP 2377, TCP/UDP 7946, and UDP 4789.
  • Review the manager and worker firewall policies separately before changing them.
  • The spread placement preference is not a hard guarantee. Confirm placement with docker service ps.

docs.title: 12. Completion checklist
docs.text:
Requested item Verified result Docker installed and Swarm available Verified on both nodes Ryzen 0 configured as manager Manager is leader Ryzen 1 joined as worker Worker is Ready and Active Private Docker Registry Running; Registry API returned HTTP 200 Docker Swarm Visualizer Running; displayed both nodes Test Compose application Deployed with 2/2 replicas Multi-node placement One task observed on each node Client application access Both Nebula endpoints returned HTTP 200

Verification date: November 3, 2026.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: A bare Lenovo ThinkCentre M715q, plugged into the university campus network and booted from the bootstrap USB stick, reaches the point where remote-config provisioning takes over. The unattended install itself is covered on the Operating System page.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A campus network drop (RJ45).
  • From university IT: DHCP and outbound HTTPS on that drop.
  • A USB stick.
  • A Linux machine to build the iPXE USB image.

docs.title: Design decisions
docs.text:
• The process is codified and repeatable. Nothing in it is machine-specific — hostnames, credentials, and configuration all derive from the remote config in this repository — so it scales to any number of boxes.
  • Commodity small-form-factor hardware. The Lenovo ThinkCentre M715q is inexpensive, quiet, and fits campus desk space.
  • The USB stick is the only physical bootstrap medium. It carries a minimal embedded script that chains to this repository; see the Operating System page for why the boot logic lives in the repository rather than on the stick.

docs.title: The hardware
docs.text:
Lenovo ThinkCentre M715q.

Specifications (CPU, RAM, SSD, NIC) — to be researched and documented.

docs.title: Building the boot USB
docs.text:
On a Linux machine, install the build dependencies and build iPXE with usb.ipxe embedded:

sudo apt install syslinux-common mtools syslinux
git clone https://github.com/ipxe/ipxe.git
cd ipxe/src
make bin-x86_64-efi/ipxe.usb EMBED=<path to paceuniversity-cs371>/provisioning/usb.ipxe

Rename the resulting bin-x86_64-efi/ipxe.usb to cs371-bootstrap.img for easier tool compatibility, then flash it to a USB stick:

  • Windows: Rufus or balenaEtcher
  • Linux: dd

docs.title: Connecting to the campus network
docs.text:
Plug the machine into a campus network drop via RJ45. The drop must provide DHCP and allow outbound HTTPS.

What to request from IT, and how — to be researched and documented.

docs.title: Booting from the USB
docs.text:
Insert the USB stick and boot the machine from it (boot order or one-time boot menu). Disable Secure Boot if necessary.

Document the exact M715q firmware steps (boot menu key, boot order settings, Secure Boot) — to be researched and documented after the first boot test.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
The first boot test on the Lenovo hardware is still pending. Expected results:

  1. The machine powers on and boots from the USB stick.
  2. iPXE obtains a DHCP lease and fetches bootstrap.ipxe from GitHub.
  3. The Ubuntu installer starts — from here the Operating System page takes over.

docs.title: Setting up Nebula Lighthouse
docs.text:
AWS EC2 t2.nano:

$ uname -srmo
Linux 6.14.0-1014-aws x86_64 GNU/Linux

$ cat /etc/os-release
PRETTY_NAME="Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS"
NAME="Ubuntu"
VERSION_ID="24.04"
VERSION="24.04.3 LTS (Noble Numbat)"
VERSION_CODENAME=noble
ID=ubuntu
ID_LIKE=debian
HOME_URL="https://www.ubuntu.com/"
SUPPORT_URL="https://help.ubuntu.com/"
BUG_REPORT_URL="https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/"
PRIVACY_POLICY_URL="https://www.ubuntu.com/legal/terms-and-policies/privacy-policy"
UBUNTU_CODENAME=noble
LOGO=ubuntu-logo

Allocated storage:

$ df -hT / /data
Filesystem     Type  Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/root      ext4   96G  8.3G   88G   9% /
/dev/xvdbb     ext4  196G   28K  186G   1% /data

Download the official archive and checksum file to /tmp:

curl -fL -o /tmp/nebula-linux-amd64.tar.gz https://github.com/slackhq/nebula/releases/download/v1.11.2/nebula-linux-amd64.tar.gz
curl -fL -o /tmp/nebula-SHASUM256.txt https://github.com/slackhq/nebula/releases/download/v1.11.2/SHASUM256.txt

-rw-rw-r-- 1 ubuntu ubuntu  18M Oct 17 18:22 nebula-linux-amd64.tar.gz
-rw-rw-r-- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 6.7K Oct 17 18:22 nebula-SHASUM256.txt

Verify the downloaded archive against the official checksum:

cd /tmp && grep ' nebula-linux-amd64.tar.gz$' nebula-SHASUM256.txt | sha256sum -c -

Expected result:

nebula-linux-amd64.tar.gz: OK

Extract the verified archive into its own temporary directory:

mkdir -p /tmp/nebula-v1.11.2
tar -xzf /tmp/nebula-linux-amd64.tar.gz -C /tmp/nebula-v1.11.2

Inspect the extracted files before installing them:

$ ls -la /tmp/nebula-v1.11.2
total 35824
drwxrwxr-x  2 ubuntu ubuntu     4096 Oct 17 18:26 .
drwxrwxrwt 13 root   root      20480 Oct 17 18:26 ..
-rwxr-xr-x  1 ubuntu ubuntu 26317909 Sep 22 13:02 nebula
-rwxr-xr-x  1 ubuntu ubuntu 10336960 Sep 22 13:02 nebula-cert

docs.title: Install the two Nebula binaries into /usr/local/bin:
docs.text:
sudo install -o root -g root -m 0755 /tmp/nebula-v1.11.2/nebula /tmp/nebula-v1.11.2/nebula-cert /usr/local/bin/

$ ls -ltrh /usr/local/bin/

.........

-rwxr-xr-x 1 root   root    26M Oct 17 18:31 nebula
-rwxr-xr-x 1 root   root   9.9M Oct 17 18:31 nebula-cert

Verify both installed binaries and their versions:

$ /usr/local/bin/nebula -version && /usr/local/bin/nebula-cert -version
Version: 1.11.2
Version: 1.11.2

We'll run Nebula as a dedicate user nebula, let's create it:

sudo useradd --system --user-group --no-create-home --home-dir /nonexistent --shell /usr/sbin/nologin nebula

$ getent passwd nebula
nebula:x:999:987::/nonexistent:/usr/sbin/nologin

Create the configuration directory so root controls its contents while the nebula group can read them:

sudo install -d -o root -g nebula -m 0750 /etc/nebula

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Our chosen overlay subnet: 10.80.0.0/24 with the lighthouse overlay IP 10.80.0.1.

Create a protected PKI working directory in ubunbu's home:

install -d -m 0700 /home/ubuntu/nebula-pki

Generate an encrypted v2 CA:

cd /home/ubuntu/nebula-pki
nebula-cert ca -name "Nebula 10.80.0.0/24 CA" -duration 87600h -encrypt -argon-memory 65536 -argon-parallelism 2 -argon-iterations 3 -version 2

Then verify the certificates have been generated:

nebula-cert print -path /home/ubuntu/nebula-pki/ca.crt

The output should be something like:

{
    "curve": "CURVE25519",
    "details": {
        "groups": null,
        "isCa": true,
        "issuer": "",
        "name": "Nebula 10.80.0.0/24 CA",
        "networks": null,
        "notAfter": "2036-10-14T19:42:29Z",
        "notBefore": "2026-10-17T19:42:29Z",
        "unsafeNetworks": null
    },
    "fingerprint": "9423b6a87f3f196ca61ed981423b1bef03b596ea8c733a8d95d7aec9b5df8cb5",
    "publicKey": "dd78e234cbb48a31b451cfc7567fc8d4778a60008b13cc9777e555e743093fa1",
    "signature": "607bd6447070a4ee8d7147863f5c6f82236747a0e15eb3f8497a9dcb03879860928d8a114820ba47419c1cb7832d98c77e112d9713467f8f4d75ac0df6607806",
    "version": 2
}

Next, issue the lighthouse certificate:

nebula-cert sign -ca-crt ca.crt -ca-key ca.key -name "lighthouse" -networks "10.80.0.1/24" -groups "lighthouse" -duration 8760h -version 2 -out-crt lighthouse.crt -out-key lighthouse.key

Verify the lighthouse certificate:

nebula-cert print -path lighthouse.crt

{
    "curve": "CURVE25519",
    "details": {
        "groups": [
            "lighthouse"
        ],
        "isCa": false,
        "issuer": "9423b6a87f3f196ca61ed981423b1bef03b596ea8c733a8d95d7aec9b5df8cb5",
        "name": "lighthouse",
        "networks": [
            "10.80.0.1/24"
        ],
        "notAfter": "2027-10-17T19:47:39Z",
        "notBefore": "2026-10-17T19:47:39Z",
        "unsafeNetworks": null
    },
    "fingerprint": "ed873d21a84592d2a7c0a35789a5fc058270f1c68df05ab75d11697ed1c8b3f9",
    "publicKey": "832a9f2999019a7cc2dedf55e134ef5e50fa50e36b44d09a8cbde612fbd35c0a",
    "signature": "d25299d8bafa6df22275271b75ed73ecfe88a0852e3e2ceb304a88f3be11979d738cff78a66331208777e5a1c7c3cbe441bcfe15a94ee5668ac1af45119ac009",
    "version": 2
}

Install only the lighthouse’s required files into /etc/nebula. This does not copy the CA private key:

sudo install -o root -g nebula -m 0640 /home/ubuntu/nebula-pki/ca.crt /home/ubuntu/nebula-pki/lighthouse.crt /home/ubuntu/nebula-pki/lighthouse.key /etc/nebula/

The lighthouse host will provide both discover and relay services. Create the configuration file /etc/nebula/config.yml:

pki:
  ca: /etc/nebula/ca.crt
  cert: /etc/nebula/lighthouse.crt
  key: /etc/nebula/lighthouse.key
  initiating_version: 2

static_host_map: {}

lighthouse:
  am_lighthouse: true
  serve_dns: true
  dns:
    host: 10.80.0.1
    port: 53
  hosts: []

relay:
  am_relay: true
  use_relays: false
  relays: []

listen:
  host: 0.0.0.0
  port: 4242

tun:
  disabled: false
  dev: nebula1

firewall:
  outbound: []
  inbound:
    - port: 53
      proto: udp
      group: any

logging:
  level: info
  format: text

Set correct permissions on the config file:

sudo chown root:nebula /etc/nebula/config.yml
sudo chmod 0640 /etc/nebula/config.yml

Validate this new config file:

$ sudo /usr/local/bin/nebula -test -config /etc/nebula/config.yml
time=2026-10-18T18:10:06.913Z level=INFO msg="firewall:\n    inbound:\n        - group: any\n          port: 53\n          proto: udp\n    outbound: []\nlighthouse:\n    am_lighthouse: true\n    dns:\n        host: 10.80.0.1\n        port: 53\n    hosts: []\n    serve_dns: true\nlisten:\n    host: 0.0.0.0\n    port: 4242\nlogging:\n    format: text\n    level: info\npki:\n    ca: /etc/nebula/ca.crt\n    cert: /etc/nebula/lighthouse.crt\n    initiating_version: 2\n    key: /etc/nebula/lighthouse.key\nrelay:\n    am_relay: true\n    relays: []\n    use_relays: false\nstatic_host_map: {}\ntun:\n    dev: nebula1\n    disabled: false\n"
time=2026-10-18T18:10:06.918Z level=INFO msg="Firewall rule added" firewallRule="map[caName: caSha: cidr: direction:incoming endPort:53 groups:[any] host: localCidr: proto:17 startPort:53]"
time=2026-10-18T18:10:06.918Z level=INFO msg="Firewall started" firewallHashes=SHA:65bf52fb0778bf05e3b7bac9dfbed963481e710f2eeaf53d09cf1d59317bca14,FNV:715780406

time=2026-10-18T18:10:06.919Z level=INFO msg="punchy disabled"

Create the systemd service /etc/systemd/system/nebula.service:

[Unit]
Description=Nebula Lighthouse and Relay
Wants=network-online.target
After=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=nebula
Group=nebula
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/nebula -config /etc/nebula/config.yml
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_ADMIN CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_ADMIN CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
NoNewPrivileges=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=true
PrivateTmp=true

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Reload systemd so it recognizes the new service:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload

Start Nebula and check whether it started successfully:

sudo systemctl start nebula
sudo systemctl status nebula --no-pager

Type Protocol Port Source Custom UDP UDP 4242 0.0.0.0/0

docs.title: Ryzen Severs
docs.text:
The lighthouse and relay are ready. Next is issuing the six server certificates. Planned overlay addresses:

Server Nebula overlay IP ryzen-0 10.80.0.10/24 ryzen-1 10.80.0.11/24 ryzen-2 10.80.0.12/24 ryzen-3 10.80.0.13/24 ryzen-4 10.80.0.14/24 ryzen-5 10.80.0.15/24

Generate the first server certificate:

cd /home/ubuntu/nebula-pki
nebula-cert sign -ca-crt ca.crt -ca-key ca.key -name "ryzen-0" -networks "10.80.0.10/24" -groups "servers" -duration 8760h -version 2 -out-crt ryzen-0.crt -out-key ryzen-0.key
nebula-cert sign -ca-crt ca.crt -ca-key ca.key -name "ryzen-1" -networks "10.80.0.11/24" -groups "servers" -duration 8760h -version 2 -out-crt ryzen-1.crt -out-key ryzen-1.key
nebula-cert sign -ca-crt ca.crt -ca-key ca.key -name "ryzen-2" -networks "10.80.0.12/24" -groups "servers" -duration 8760h -version 2 -out-crt ryzen-2.crt -out-key ryzen-2.key
nebula-cert sign -ca-crt ca.crt -ca-key ca.key -name "ryzen-3" -networks "10.80.0.13/24" -groups "servers" -duration 8760h -version 2 -out-crt ryzen-3.crt -out-key ryzen-3.key
nebula-cert sign -ca-crt ca.crt -ca-key ca.key -name "ryzen-4" -networks "10.80.0.14/24" -groups "servers" -duration 8760h -version 2 -out-crt ryzen-4.crt -out-key ryzen-4.key
nebula-cert sign -ca-crt ca.crt -ca-key ca.key -name "ryzen-5" -networks "10.80.0.15/24" -groups "servers" -duration 8760h -version 2 -out-crt ryzen-5.crt -out-key ryzen-5.key

Verify that all six certificate/key pairs exist:

ls -l /home/ubuntu/nebula-pki/ryzen-{0..5}.{crt,key}

All six server certificate/key pairs exist with secure 0600 permissions.

-rw------- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 318 Oct 18 06:48 /home/ubuntu/nebula-pki/ryzen-0.crt
-rw------- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 127 Oct 18 06:48 /home/ubuntu/nebula-pki/ryzen-0.key
-rw------- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 318 Oct 18 07:13 /home/ubuntu/nebula-pki/ryzen-1.crt
-rw------- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 127 Oct 18 07:13 /home/ubuntu/nebula-pki/ryzen-1.key
-rw------- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 318 Oct 18 07:13 /home/ubuntu/nebula-pki/ryzen-2.crt
-rw------- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 127 Oct 18 07:13 /home/ubuntu/nebula-pki/ryzen-2.key
-rw------- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 318 Oct 18 07:13 /home/ubuntu/nebula-pki/ryzen-3.crt
-rw------- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 127 Oct 18 07:13 /home/ubuntu/nebula-pki/ryzen-3.key
-rw------- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 318 Oct 18 07:13 /home/ubuntu/nebula-pki/ryzen-4.crt
-rw------- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 127 Oct 18 07:13 /home/ubuntu/nebula-pki/ryzen-4.key
-rw------- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 318 Oct 18 07:13 /home/ubuntu/nebula-pki/ryzen-5.crt
-rw------- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 127 Oct 18 07:13 /home/ubuntu/nebula-pki/ryzen-5.key

docs.title: Generate Laptop Certificates
docs.text:
The laptop overlay IPs start at 10.80.0.100/24.

Owner ID Nebula IP Group jo14591n 10.80.0.100/24 laptops 
nebula-cert sign -ca-crt ca.crt -ca-key ca.key -name "jo14591n" -networks "10.80.0.100/24" -groups "laptops" -duration 8760h -version 2 -out-crt jo14591n.crt -out-key jo14591n.key

docs.title: Shared client configuration
docs.text: Replace <LIGHTHOUSE_PUBLIC_IP> with the EC2 Elastic IP.

docs.title: Ryzen server config
docs.text:
Use this as /etc/nebula/config.yml:

pki:
  ca: /etc/nebula/ca.crt
  cert: /etc/nebula/host.crt
  key: /etc/nebula/host.key
  initiating_version: 2

static_host_map:
  "10.80.0.1": ["<LIGHTHOUSE_PUBLIC_IP>:4242"]

lighthouse:
  am_lighthouse: false
  hosts:
    - "10.80.0.1"

relay:
  relays:
    - "10.80.0.1"
  am_relay: false
  use_relays: true

listen:
  host: 0.0.0.0
  port: 0

punchy:
  punch: true
  respond: true

tun:
  disabled: false

firewall:
  outbound:
    - port: any
      proto: any
      host: any

  inbound:
    - port: any
      proto: icmp
      host: any
    - port: 22
      proto: tcp
      group: laptops
    - port: any
      proto: any
      group: servers

logging:
  level: info
  format: text

This permits:

  • ICMP testing from overlay members.
  • SSH from certificates in the laptops group.
  • All overlay traffic between servers.
  • No other inbound overlay traffic.

docs.title: Ubuntu Ryzen server setup
docs.text:
Each server receives only:

ca.crt
ryzen-N.crt
ryzen-N.key

Rename its certificate and key to host.crt and host.key during installation.

docs.title: Install Nebula
docs.text:
cd /tmp
curl -fLO https://github.com/slackhq/nebula/releases/download/v1.11.2/nebula-linux-amd64.tar.gz
curl -fLO https://github.com/slackhq/nebula/releases/download/v1.11.2/SHASUM256.txt
grep ' nebula-linux-amd64.tar.gz$' SHASUM256.txt | sha256sum -c -
mkdir -p nebula-v1.11.2
tar -xzf nebula-linux-amd64.tar.gz -C nebula-v1.11.2
sudo install -o root -g root -m 0755 nebula-v1.11.2/nebula /usr/local/bin/nebula

The official project distributes Linux, macOS, and Windows binaries and also documents distribution packages. https://nebula.defined.net/docs/guides/quick-start/?utm_source=chatgpt.com

docs.title: Create the service account
docs.text: sudo useradd --system --user-group --no-create-home --home-dir /nonexistent --shell /usr/sbin/nologin nebula

docs.title: Install credentials
docs.text:
For ryzen-0, for example:

sudo install -d -o root -g nebula -m 0750 /etc/nebula
sudo install -o root -g nebula -m 0640 ca.crt /etc/nebula/ca.crt
sudo install -o root -g nebula -m 0640 ryzen-0.crt /etc/nebula/host.crt
sudo install -o root -g nebula -m 0640 ryzen-0.key /etc/nebula/host.key

Use the matching certificate/key on each server.

docs.title: Install and validate the configuration
docs.text:
After creating /etc/nebula/config.yml from the server template:

sudo chown root:nebula /etc/nebula/config.yml
sudo chmod 0640 /etc/nebula/config.yml
sudo /usr/local/bin/nebula -test -config /etc/nebula/config.yml

docs.title: Create the systemd service
docs.text:
Create /etc/systemd/system/nebula.service:

[Unit]
Description=Nebula Overlay Client
Wants=network-online.target
After=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=nebula
Group=nebula
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/nebula -config /etc/nebula/config.yml
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_ADMIN
CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_ADMIN
NoNewPrivileges=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=true
PrivateTmp=true

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

CAP_NET_ADMIN lets the unprivileged service create and configure its TUN interface. https://nebula.defined.net/docs/guides/running-nebula-as-non-root/?utm_source=chatgpt.com

Start it:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now nebula
sudo systemctl status nebula --no-pager

docs.title: Laptop Configuration
docs.text:
A laptop receives:

ca.crt
<slack_id>.crt
<slack_id>.key

Use this client policy:

lighthouse:
  am_lighthouse: false
  hosts:
    - "10.80.0.1"

relay:
  relays:
    - "10.80.0.1"
  am_relay: false
  use_relays: true

listen:
  host: 0.0.0.0
  port: 0

punchy:
  punch: true
  respond: true

tun:
  disabled: false

firewall:
  outbound:
    - port: any
      proto: any
      host: any

  inbound:
    - port: any
      proto: icmp
      group: servers

logging:
  level: info
  format: text

Replace the three uppercase file placeholders with platform-specific absolute paths below.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
brew install nebula
nebula -version

The official repository documents Homebrew installation. https://github.com/slackhq/nebula?utm_source=chatgpt.com

The version must be at least 1.10 because these are v2 certificates.

docs.title: Install credentials
docs.text:
sudo install -d -o root -g wheel -m 0700 /etc/nebula
sudo install -o root -g wheel -m 0600 ca.crt /etc/nebula/ca.crt
sudo install -o root -g wheel -m 0600 <slack_id>.crt /etc/nebula/host.crt
sudo install -o root -g wheel -m 0600 <slack_id>.key /etc/nebula/host.key

Use these paths in the configuration:

pki:
  ca: /etc/nebula/ca.crt
  cert: /etc/nebula/host.crt
  key: /etc/nebula/host.key

Save the complete laptop configuration as /etc/nebula/config.yml, then:

sudo chmod 0600 /etc/nebula/config.yml
sudo nebula -test -config /etc/nebula/config.yml
sudo nebula -service install -config /etc/nebula/config.yml
sudo nebula -service start

docs.title: Install files
docs.text:
Download the official nebula-windows-amd64.zip for v1.11.2 and extract nebula.exe to:

C:\Program Files\Nebula\nebula.exe

Place the credentials in:

C:\ProgramData\Nebula\ca.crt
C:\ProgramData\Nebula\host.crt
C:\ProgramData\Nebula\host.key

Save the configuration as:

C:\ProgramData\Nebula\config.yml

Use absolute Windows paths:

pki:
  ca: "C:\\ProgramData\\Nebula\\ca.crt"
  cert: "C:\\ProgramData\\Nebula\\host.crt"
  key: "C:\\ProgramData\\Nebula\\host.key"
  initiating_version: 2

Absolute paths are important because the Windows service does not use the interactive shell’s working directory. https://github.com/slackhq/nebula/issues/1140?utm_source=chatgpt.com

docs.title: Validate and install the service
docs.text:
Run PowerShell as Administrator:

& 'C:\Program Files\Nebula\nebula.exe' -test -config 'C:\ProgramData\Nebula\config.yml'
& 'C:\Program Files\Nebula\nebula.exe' -service install -config 'C:\ProgramData\Nebula\config.yml'
& 'C:\Program Files\Nebula\nebula.exe' -service start
Get-Service Nebula

Nebula’s Windows service supports -service install and -service start. https://github.com/slackhq/nebula/discussions/1089?utm_source=chatgpt.com

docs.title: Connectivity test
docs.text:
After one Ryzen server and one laptop are running:

ping 10.80.0.10
ssh <server-user>@10.80.0.10
ssh <server-user>@ryzen-0

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Establish secure remote connectivity between the CS371 Ryzen servers and student laptops using Nebula VPN.

The network mesh allows students to administer their Linux servers from different networks without exposing SSH directly to the public internet.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Lenovo ThinkCentre M715q running Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS
  • MacBook running macOS
  • Internet connectivity on both devices
  • Nebula VPN v1.11.2 installed on both devices
  • Nebula certificates and private keys provided for each device
  • Access to the CS371 Nebula lighthouse
  • OpenSSH server configured on Ubuntu
  • SSH public-key authentication

docs.title: Design decisions
docs.text:
We selected Nebula VPN to establish encrypted connectivity between devices across different networks.

The network uses the following Nebula IP addresses:

Device Nebula IP Role Lighthouse 10.80.0.1 Peer discovery Ryzen (ryzen-0) 10.80.0.10 Linux server MacBook (bayron) 10.80.0.101 Remote administration

The Ryzen runs Nebula as a systemd service, while the MacBook currently runs Nebula manually.

SSH access is restricted through Nebula firewall rules.

docs.title: 1. Install Nebula
docs.text:
Install Nebula v1.11.2 on the Ryzen and MacBook.

Place the appropriate certificate, private key, and CA certificate in /etc/nebula/ on each device.

Never commit private keys or certificates containing sensitive information to GitHub.

docs.title: 2. Configure Nebula
docs.text:
Both devices use /etc/nebula/config.yml.

The configuration includes the lighthouse, device certificates, VPN interface, and firewall rules.

The Ryzen's inbound firewall configuration includes:

firewall:
  outbound:
    - port: any
      proto: any
      host: any

  inbound:
    - port: any
      proto: icmp
      host: any

    - port: 22
      proto: tcp
      host: bayron

    - port: 22
      proto: tcp
      group: servers

The host: bayron rule matches the MacBook's Nebula certificate identity.

docs.title: 3. Start Nebula on Ubuntu
docs.text:
sudo systemctl enable nebula
sudo systemctl restart nebula
sudo systemctl status nebula

docs.title: 4. Start Nebula on macOS
docs.text:
sudo nebula -config /etc/nebula/config.yml

Keep this process running while using the VPN.

docs.title: Test Nebula connectivity
docs.text:
From the MacBook:

ping -c 4 10.80.0.10

Expected result: Successful ICMP replies.

docs.title: Test SSH connectivity
docs.text:
nc -vz -w 5 10.80.0.10 22

Expected result:

Connection to 10.80.0.10 port 22 [tcp/ssh] succeeded!

docs.title: Connect remotely
docs.text:
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 milkalmond@10.80.0.10

Expected result:

milkalmond@cs371-bc9b0c:~$

Remote SSH connectivity was successfully verified from a separate internet connection outside the home network.

docs.title: SSH connection timed out
docs.text:
Initially, Nebula ICMP ping succeeded, but SSH connections to port 22 timed out.

We enabled debug logging and inspected the Ryzen's Nebula logs:

sudo journalctl -u nebula --since "10 minutes ago" --no-pager

The logs reported:

dropping inbound packet
reason="no matching rule in firewall table"

The original firewall configuration used:

groups:
  - laptops
  - servers

This required the connecting peer to match both groups.

We corrected the configuration by using the MacBook's certificate identity:

- port: 22
  proto: tcp
  host: bayron

After restarting Nebula, TCP port 22 became reachable and SSH authentication succeeded.

docs.title: SSH key authentication
docs.text:
The SSH private key must be available on the client device initiating the connection.

For this setup, the private key is stored on the MacBook at:

~/.ssh/id_ed25519

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text: Private keys must not be uploaded to the repository. Any previously exposed Nebula private keys should be rotated before production or sensitive use.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: A Lenovo ThinkCentre M715q, booted from the bootstrap USB on campus Ethernet, installs Ubuntu 24.04.5 Server unattended onto its SSD and comes up reachable over SSH with the hostname cs371-<last 6 hex digits of its Ethernet MAC>.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Campus Ethernet with DHCP and outbound HTTPS.
  • The flashed cs371-bootstrap.img USB stick. Physical and firmware steps (USB boot order, Secure Boot) are covered on the Hardware page.

docs.title: Design decisions
docs.text:
• The USB stick carries only a minimal embedded iPXE script (provisioning/usb.ipxe) that chains to the GitHub-hosted provisioning/bootstrap.ipxe. Boot logic can be revised in this repository without reflashing any USB sticks.
  • Ubuntu autoinstall with a NoCloud seed served from this repository. bootstrap.ipxe boots the Ubuntu 24.04.5 live-server installer over the network and points it at the raw GitHub URL of provisioning/autoinstall/, so the entire install is unattended and reproducible from this repository alone.
  • SSH key-only access. The installer creates the admin user with a locked password and allow-pw: false; the only way in is the authorized SSH key.
  • MAC-derived hostname. Each machine names itself cs371- plus the last 6 hex digits of its Ethernet MAC, guaranteeing unique, predictable hostnames with no per-machine configuration.

docs.title: Installation and configuration
docs.text: Building and flashing the boot USB is covered on the Hardware page.

docs.title: Boot flow
docs.text: USB → iPXE → bootstrap.ipxe (GitHub) → Ubuntu installer → Autoinstall

docs.title: Provisioning files
docs.text:
provisioning/
├── usb.ipxe
├── bootstrap.ipxe
└── autoinstall/
    ├── user-data
    └── meta-data
  • usb.ipxe — embedded in the USB image. Obtains a DHCP lease and chains to the current bootstrap.ipxe on GitHub.
  • bootstrap.ipxe — downloads the Ubuntu 24.04.5 netboot kernel and initrd from https://releases.ubuntu.com/24.04.5, boots the live-server ISO over HTTPS, and passes autoinstall ds=nocloud-net with the seed URL pointing at this repository's provisioning/autoinstall/. The set semicolon:hex 3b line embeds the literal ; that the NoCloud datasource syntax requires in the kernel command line.
  • autoinstall/user-data — the autoinstall configuration:
    • creates the milkalmond user with a locked password ("!");
    • installs the SSH server with password login disabled and public-key authentication enabled;
    • installs Ubuntu directly to the SSD (storage: layout: name: direct);
    • installs git and curl;
    • in late-commands, derives the hostname from the default-route interface's MAC address and writes it into /target/etc/hostname and /target/etc/hosts;
    • creates /target/etc/issue.d/ip.issue so the current IPv4 address is displayed on the console login screen.
  • autoinstall/meta-data — empty, but must exist for the NoCloud datasource to accept the seed.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Our team completed a full provisioning test on the Lenovo Ryzen hardware.

  1. The machine successfully booted from the USB, iPXE obtained a DHCP lease, and fetched bootstrap.ipxe from GitHub.
  2. The installer downloaded the Ubuntu 24.04.5 kernel, initrd, and live-server ISO from releases.ubuntu.com and completed the autoinstall.
  3. The machine rebooted successfully as cs371-bc9b0c, generated from the last six hexadecimal digits of the Ethernet MAC address 6c:4b:90:bc:9b:0c.
  4. Ubuntu 24.04.5 rejected the originally configured admin username because it is reserved by the system. Our team changed the autoinstall username to milkalmond, which allowed provisioning to complete successfully.
  5. SSH public-key authentication to milkalmond@cs371-bc9b0c was successfully verified from a separate laptop.
  6. Password-based SSH authentication was tested separately and correctly returned Permission denied (publickey).
  7. The console IP display was successfully tested using /etc/issue.d/ip.issue. After DHCP completed, the login screen displayed the machine's current IPv4 address, allowing the SSH destination to be identified without checking the DHCP server or router.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problems encountered and how we resolved them.
